summary: Specifies how hosts can offer ISO transport services on top of TCP, reserving TCP port 102 for it. This is version 3 of the protocol and replaces RFC 983, with changes that are minor but incompatible. The RFC was an Internet standard and was later updated by RFC 2126.

eli5.summary: Another network's messages need a ride on the Internet's trucks. This memo says how to pack them, and which loading dock to use, so both sides understand.

subtitle: How to run ISO transport service over a TCP connection, so ISO applications could be tried out on the Internet.

tldr.problem: ISO and CCITT session, presentation and application protocols were hard to try out on the Internet because the ISO lower layers were still immature, while TCP/IP was stable and widely available.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC runs the ISO transport class 0 protocol over a TCP connection to port 102, wrapping each ISO transport message in a small 4-octet TPKT header that marks where it ends in the byte stream.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (version 3) that obsoletes RFC 983 and is incompatible with it. It has been updated by RFC 2126.

today: RFC 1006 is an Internet Standard. It obsoletes RFC 983 and has been updated by RFC 2126.

sections.title: Why Put ISO Transport on TCP
sections.content:
RFC 1006 describes how hosts on the Internet can offer ISO transport services on top of TCP. The authors wanted ISO and CCITT session, presentation and application protocols to be usable in the ARPA Internet without disrupting existing facilities. This would let people gain experience with those protocols and help a graceful move from TCP/IP-based networks to ISO-based ones.

The idea relies on layer independence: if a layer keeps the services it offers, the layer above does not care which protocol runs underneath. So the memo presents a Transport Service Access Point (TSAP) that looks the same as the ISO one in ISO 8072, but implements the ISO class 0 transport protocol (TP0) over TCP and IP rather than over an ISO network protocol. Higher ISO layers can then run without knowing they sit on a TCP/IP internet.

This is version 3 of the protocol. It supersedes RFC 983, and the changes are described as minor but unfortunately incompatible.
sections.eli5: Imagine a toy that only fits one kind of building block. This memo is an adapter so the toy can use the blocks everyone already has, and the toy never notices.

sections.title: Motivation and Migration Strategy
sections.content:
The memo gives two arguments for joining the two protocol suites at the transport layer. First, good implementations of the ISO lower layers were taking as long to appear as the higher ones, so higher-level protocols were not being pursued; TCP/IP is mature and offers essentially identical functionality, so it is an ideal medium for developing them. Second, gateways at the IP and ISO IP layers would probably not be useful in the long run, because every Internet host would need to support both TP4 and TCP.

Both arguments point to doing the join exactly at the transport service access point, which maximizes the number of ISO layers that can be developed.

The memo says it is not a migration or intercept document. A transition plan is completely beyond its scope, though the protocol might form part of one.
sections.eli5: It is easier to test new toys on a playground that already exists than to build a new playground first. TCP/IP was the playground that already worked.

sections.title: The Model and Its Primitives
sections.content:
The model has a TS-user (a process using the transport service) talking through the ISO TSAP interface to a TS-provider, the black-box that implements this memo. The provider in turn uses the TCP interface from RFC 793. A process that implements the protocol is a TS-peer.

All aspects of the ISO transport service definition (ISO 8072) are supported except Quality of Service parameters, which are left for further study. The ISO standards do not define the format of a TSAP ID, so the memo requires the GOSIP specification for interpreting it.

The ISO TSAP has no built-in client/server model. Instead of a server listening on a well-known port, the provider raises an INDICATION event when a connection arrives, and users sit idle until they issue a REQUEST or accept an INDICATION.

The memo assumes TCP offers events (connected, connect fails, data ready, errored, closed) and actions (listen on port, open port, read data, send data, close). It uses these to emulate the network service primitives class 0 needs (N-CONNECT, N-DATA, N-DISCONNECT) and so offers the T-CONNECT, T-DATA, T-EXPEDITED DATA and T-DISCONNECT primitives to the TS-user.
sections.eli5: The program on top just says "send this" and "hang up." The adapter quietly turns those requests into TCP actions underneath.

sections.title: How the Protocol Runs over TCP
sections.content:
The protocol is identical to ISO transport class 0 with four exceptions. For testing, initial data may be exchanged during connection establishment. For testing, an expedited data service is supported. For performance, a much larger TSDU size is supported. And the network service is provided by TCP.

Connecting. To make a connection, the TS-peer performs an active open to the desired IP address using TCP port 102. A server listens on TCP port 102; when a client connects, the event occurs and an implicit N-CONNECT.RESPONSE is performed. The default TPDU size is 65531 octets instead of 128, and a smaller standard size can be negotiated with the mechanism in ISO 8073. Expedited data is off by default and can be negotiated in the connection request and confirmation.

Transferring data. To send, the peer builds a TPKT and uses the TCP send primitive. To receive, TCP signals data ready and a TPKT is read. If expedited data was negotiated, it travels in a modified ED TPDU on the same TCP connection as everything else.

Releasing. An N-DISCONNECT.REQUEST is just closing the TCP connection. If TCP reports the connection closed or errored, that is an N-DISCONNECT.INDICATION.
sections.eli5: Both sides meet at the same loading dock, number 102. To talk, they put messages in labelled boxes. To say goodbye, they simply hang up the phone.

sections.title: The TPKT Packet Format
sections.content:
TCP is a continuous stream of octets with no boundaries, but class 0 expects discrete units. The memo adds a simple packetization scheme: each packet, called a TPKT, is a header plus one TPDU. Transport class 0 never combines several TPDUs in one unit, so a network service data unit is the same as a TPDU here.

The header has the same format for every packet type. It holds a vrsn field, always 3 for this version, a reserved octet, and a 16-bit packet length counting the whole packet including the header, with a minimum of 7 and a maximum of 65535. That allows a maximum TPDU size of 65531 octets and, based on the size of the data transfer (DT) TPDU, a maximum TSDU size of 65524 octets.

The TPDU format is defined in ISO 8073, and only class 0 formats are exchanged. For expedited data the memo permits a non-standard ED TPDU, nearly identical to DT except for its code. Its credit field is zero on output and ignored on input, and the high-order bit of the TPDU-NR and EOT octet marks the end of a TSDU. The TP specification limits an expedited data unit to 16 octets.
sections.eli5: A stream of bytes is like water in a pipe, with no way to tell where one message ends. The TPKT header is a label on each bottle of water saying how big the bottle is.

sections.title: Version History and Comments
sections.content:
The authors note that since RFC 983 appeared in April 1986 they gained much experience. Version 2 of the protocol came in September 1986, based mostly on community comments. In January 1987 they observed that version 2 differed only slightly from the actual transport class 0 definition. TP0 is meant to run over a reliable network service such as X.25, and TCP can provide that, so the memo really just describes a way of encapsulating TP0 inside TCP.

The changes from version 1 to version 2 and then version 3 are all relatively small. They came about because version 1 already used the TPDU formats of the ISO transport protocol.
sections.eli5: The inventors kept tweaking the design and finally noticed it was almost the same as an existing recipe, just cooked in a different pot.

fields.name: packet length
fields.desc: Length of the whole packet in octets, including this header; minimum 7, maximum 65535.
